book: 258 - South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today

chapters.relation: Peter Fosl reads Metallica lyrics through Nietzsche's and Marx's critiques of Christianity: 'Leper Messiah' and 'The God that Failed' cast religion as a slave morality born of ressentiment and as Marx's 'opium' that pacifies the exploited. He asks whether Metallica achieves Nietzsche's transvaluation of values or stays trapped in 'incomplete nihilism' - songs like 'One' and 'To Live is to Die' longing nostalgically for the God that failed - while 'Escape' and 'The Four Horsemen' point toward a life-affirming overcoming of Christianity.

Robert Sharp maps Battlestar Galactica's Cylon uprising onto Nietzsche's slave revolt in morality. The enslaved Cylons, like Nietzsche's early Christians under Rome, invent the concept of a soul and a single loving God to invert their masters' master morality, turning powerlessness (meekness, equality, faith) into virtue. Through Leoben's preaching to Starbuck and the Cylons' commune-like equality versus the Colonials' Greek-style polytheistic hierarchy, Sharp shows the powerless creating new values out of resentment to overturn those in power.

chapters.file: ch33 - The Viewer and the Look.md
chapters.relation: Meyer and Schneider use The Office's mockumentary camera to dramatize Sartre's 'the Look' and bad faith. Pam pretends she cannot choose between Roy and Jim (bad faith as being-in-itself), and is shamed when the camera catches her watching Jim and Karen; David Brent's prideful self-promotion tries and fails to control the Other's gaze. They tie the ever-present camera to the Foucault/Bentham panopticon: Jan, Dwight, and Angela police themselves because they might be watched, making the viewer complicit in the workers' existential crises.

chapters.file: ch34 - Determinism and the Dark Knight.md
chapters.relation: David Hart explains Batman's origin through Heidegger's Being and Time: Bruce Wayne is a 'thrown-project' whose world (like Alfred's butlering) shows up through chosen possibilities. Witnessing his parents' murder confronts Bruce with Angst and being-toward-death, and in Miller's Year One the bat crashing through the window lets him authentically choose 'I shall become a bat.' Hart argues this dissolves the free-will/determinism binary - Bruce's choice is neither causally compelled by trauma nor wholly unconditioned, but an authentic self-determination amid thrown possibilities.

chapters.file: ch35 - You’re Basically “a Stuffed Animal Made by Grandma”.md
chapters.relation: Renee Kyle contrasts Dr. House's detached 'doctor knows best' justice ethic with Dr. Cameron's feminist ethic of care drawn from Carol Gilligan's In a Different Voice. Cameron builds trusting relationships, sees patients as embedded in social networks, and refuses to deceive or bully (as with Ezra and the newborns in 'Maternity'), whereas House treats patients as abstract puzzle-pieces. Kyle also voices the feminist worry that valorizing care can lead women to care at personal cost, as when Cameron's own grief over her dead husband derails her professional judgment.

Bonnie Mann reads the Twilight saga through Beauvoir's The Second Sex. Bella embodies the 'relative being' who orbits Edward like a satellite, a self-sacrificing girl who loses Husserl's 'I can' body and exists only through the constant, faithful male gaze that confers meaning. Mann traces a buried feminist subtext - Bella's demand to 'be Superman too' and her transformation into a strong, agentive vampire - but argues Meyer ultimately reinstates the old promise that a woman gains existence through self-annihilation in a man, making the books' success cause for despair.

chapters.file: ch37 - Family Guy Must Die! Long Live Family Guy!.md
chapters.relation: J. Jeremy Wisnewski stages a mock threat to 'kill' the Griffins to expose Family Guy as postmodernism incarnate. Its blizzard of equal-footing references (Hitler beside Scooby-Doo) illustrates Baudrillard's hyperreal where 'the real is no longer real,' and its relentless mockery of religion, war, and politics enacts Lyotard's incredulity toward meta-narratives. Worrying this breeds cynical conservatism, he rescues the show via Foucault's power/knowledge: like Foucault's activism, one can be incredulous toward grand stories yet still fight local battles - a little incredulity is exactly what we need.

chapters.file: ch39 - Gaining Trust from the Past.md
chapters.relation: Richard Davies treats the Oceanic 815 survivors of Lost as a real state of nature, playing on the characters named Locke, Rousseau, and Hume. The scarce-water and asthma-inhaler disputes are 'tragedies of the commons,' and Sawyer's 'finders keepers' embodies a Hobbesian 'Trust No. 1' while Hurley and Jack lean toward Rousseauian 'Innocence.' Using game theory's repeated prisoners' dilemma and 'tit-for-tat,' Davies argues a Lockean state of nature (opening with cooperation) rather than a doomed Hobbesian one lets the survivors build a commonwealth against the Others.

Michael Bray argues the American Office does register class - precisely as a 'salaried mass' whose identity lies in denying class difference. Through Marx's account of surplus value and the degradation of rationalized labor (Stanley's 'run-out-the-clock,' Pam's deadened art, Michael's condo as consumer coffin), the office workers are alienated and secretly long for downsizing that never frees them. Bray invokes Benjamin to suggest Michael Scott's gap-ridden failure to be professional or private embodies what little 'authentic humanity' capitalism leaves, standing on the edge of naming the class it never names.

Donal O'Mathuna uses 24's Jack Bauer to dissect the ethics of torture, centering on Henry Shue's utilitarian 'ticking bomb' argument that torturing the bomber to save thousands is justified. He weighs deontology (torture treats persons as mere means) and virtue ethics (it degrades torturers like Agent Burke) against the utilitarian case, and shows the show itself refutes the argument: torture didn't get Fayed's bombs, innocents like Audrey Raines get caught, torturers are ruined, and Shue himself recanted - so the sanitized ticking-bomb fantasy misrepresents real, degrading torture.

Jeremy Pierce asks whether X-Men's mutants are literally a race. He rejects biological race: human genetic variation between 'races' is tiny (far below animal subspecies), and mutants, drawn from every ethnicity with a diverse X-Gene present even in non-mutants, are even less a biological group. Turning to race as a social reality (like money or Genosha's gene-tested 'Genejoke' slaves echoing US slavery), he argues mutants are 'racelike' - a useful metaphorical analogy for real racial oppression - but, being multiracial and power-defined, not strictly a race.

chapters.file: ch44 - “How Could Anyone Fall in Love with a Toaster ” Cylons as Persons.md
chapters.relation: James McRae reads Battlestar Galactica through Zen Buddhism: the fleet's annihilation and constant death illustrate the Four Noble Truths' duhkha, arising from ignorant attachment and violating interdependent arising (no-self and impermanence). Cylon death-and-resurrection parallels karma and rebirth ('all of this has happened before'), Leoben acts as a koan-wielding roshi unsettling Starbuck's assumptions, and Nishida's kenotic God as Absolute Nothingness matches the Cylons' 'we're all God.' Because Cylons feel pain, suffer cognitively, and earn karma, McRae concludes they are persons capable of satori who should seek compassionate reconciliation with humans.

Ruff and Barris cast Dr. House's rude, rule-breaking rhetoric as a form of Zen practice, working like a koan that unsettles everyone's (and House's own) habitual sense so genuine sense can emerge. In cases like 'DNR,' 'Mob Rules,' and 'House vs. God,' his 'everybody lies' provocations strip away presuppositions until the true problem reveals itself, making his irresponsibility a way of acting ethically, establishing naked intimacy, finding truth, and healing. Invoking Suzuki and 'beginner's mind,' they argue House is nondualistically inside the rhetoric, at peace once the insight arrives.

chapters.file: ch46 - Chapter 31 The Tao of the Bat.md
chapters.relation: In a mock interview with 'Bat-Tzu' (a disguised Alfred), Mark White explains Taoism through Batman. Bruce is dangerously dominated by yang after his parents' deaths and needs the yin balance that Robin (Dick as the lighthearted 'Batman with a feminine side') and his spiritual quest restore; Batman's fear-inducing shadow illustrates Lao-Tzu's usefulness of nothingness. Alfred is the Taoist sage embodying wei-wu-wei - 'action without action' - quietly serving like Chuang-Tzu's effortless butcher and like water that wears down stone, harmonizing Bruce's warring opposites toward the Way.

Jonathan and Jerry Walls read Harry Potter's Deathly Hallows through the question of death and afterlife. Harry's willing death-march models Heidegger's authenticity and being-toward-death, while Voldemort's terror of death makes him inauthentic. At King's Cross the maimed Voldemort-soul embodies William James's 'sow a character, reap a destiny': having refused remorse, he has become evil beyond repair, whereas the repentant Dumbledore has grown. Against Heidegger's atheism, Rowling's Christian resurrection imagery, backed by Locke on memory-identity, Kant, and Pascal, makes our character-forming choices infinitely consequential.

chapters.file: ch49 - House and the Life of Reason.md
chapters.relation: Henry Jacoby argues that despite House's line that we are 'selfish, base animals crawling across the Earth,' House lives a meaningful life. Rejecting God-, soul-, and afterlife-based meaning (House's Euthyphro-style objections and his '97 Seconds' near-death experiment), Jacoby locates meaning in the Socratic examined life and Aristotle's life of reason as humanity's proper function. House's relentless curiosity and puzzle-solving, tied to action and to saving lives, exemplify reason governing desire and yield eudaimonia - so 'doing things changes things,' and House, however miserable he seems, leads the examined, meaningful life.

holes.name: The Metaphysics of Race (biological vs. social race)
holes.what: The debate over whether race is a real biological kind, a socially constructed reality, or an illusion.
holes.why: Chapter 42 argues mutants are not a biological race but are 'racelike' as a social reality, and the taxonomy has specific race concepts (racial-contract, double-consciousness, intersectionality) but no general concept for the metaphysics/social-construction of race itself.
